lead: A reciprocating pump is a positive-displacement machine: a piston slides inside a cylinder, traps a fixed volume of water, and pushes it out through a one-way valve. Because the volume per stroke is fixed by the cylinder size, the ideal flow depends only on geometry and running speed. Real flow always differs a little, and the gap between ideal and real is called slip. You meet these pumps in hand pumps, pressure washers, boiler feed and high-pressure jetting, where a small steady flow at a high head is wanted.
prereq: You need: crank-and-connecting-rod motion from Unit 2, Fluid Kinematics, and pressure ideas from Unit 1, Fluid Properties and Fluid Statics.

blocks.text: Four parts do the work: a cylinder, a piston or plunger inside it, a crank turned by a motor, and a connecting rod that turns the crank's circle into the piston's back-and-forth motion. Two one-way valves sit on the cylinder head: a suction valve from the suction pipe and a delivery valve to the delivery pipe. Pressure difference alone opens and closes them; no cam touches them.

items: Suction stroke: the crank pulls the piston outward, cylinder pressure falls below atmospheric, the suction valve lifts, and water rises up the suction pipe.
Delivery stroke: the crank pushes the piston inward, the suction valve shuts, pressure rises above the delivery pressure, the delivery valve lifts, and water is pushed into the delivery pipe.

blocks.text: A piston carries rings and seals against the bore. A plunger is a plain solid ram sliding through a packed gland; plunger pumps are picked for very high heads such as boiler feed. In a single-acting pump water touches one face only, giving one suction and one delivery stroke per revolution. In a double-acting pump water touches both faces, giving two deliveries per revolution and a steadier flow; the piston rod takes up area a<sub>r</sub> on one face, so that side sweeps less volume.
Volume swept in one stroke is A L. A single-acting pump delivers that volume N/60 times a second, since N is in revolutions per minute and one revolution gives one delivery.

blocks.where: Q<sub>th</sub> is the ideal discharge in m³/s; A is the piston face area = πD²/4 in m², with D the bore in m; L is the stroke = 2 × crank radius in m; N is the crank speed in rpm; 60 converts minutes to seconds.

a<sub>r</sub> is the rod cross-section area = πd<sub>r</sub>²/4 in m², with d<sub>r</sub> the rod diameter in m; per revolution one face sweeps A L and the rod face sweeps (A − a<sub>r</sub>)L, so the sum is (2A − a<sub>r</sub>)L. Double-acting pump.

blocks.text: The flow is not steady. Piston speed follows the crank and peaks at mid-stroke, so the instantaneous discharge rises and falls twice per revolution in a double-acting pump and once in a single-acting one. That unevenness is why air vessels are fitted (see 7.8).
Slip is what geometry promises minus what the meter measures.
slip = Q<sub>th</sub> − Q<sub>act</sub> ,   C<sub>d</sub> = Q<sub>act</sub> / Q<sub>th</sub>
blocks.where: Q<sub>act</sub> is the measured discharge in m³/s; C<sub>d</sub> is the coefficient of discharge, dimensionless, also called volumetric efficiency; percentage slip = (Q<sub>th</sub> − Q<sub>act</sub>)/Q<sub>th</sub> × 100, so slip fraction = 1 − C<sub>d</sub>.

blocks.text: Positive slip is normal: Q<sub>act</sub> is less than Q<sub>th</sub> because water leaks past valves and rings, valves lag before seating, dissolved air cushions the stroke, and at high speed the cylinder does not fill completely.

Negative slip means Q<sub>act</sub> beats Q<sub>th</sub>. It happens when the suction pipe is long and the pump runs slowly: the moving water column has enough inertia to keep entering after the piston has begun its delivery stroke, so a little extra water spills through the delivery valve. A pump with a head on its suction side can also show it.

sections.h3: Work, power and the indicator diagram

blocks.text: The indicator diagram plots cylinder pressure against the volume swept over one revolution. For an ideal pump with no friction and no acceleration, the suction stroke is a flat line at suction pressure and the delivery stroke a flat line at delivery pressure; the rectangle between them is the work per stroke.
W = ρ g A L (h<sub>d</sub> + h<sub>s</sub>) ,   P = ρ g Q<sub>th</sub> (h<sub>d</sub> + h<sub>s</sub>) / 1000
blocks.where: W is work per stroke in J; P is the ideal power in kW; ρ = 1000 kg/m³ is water density; g = 9.81 m/s²; h<sub>d</sub> is the delivery height above the pump centre line in m; h<sub>s</sub> is the suction lift below the pump centre line in m; both are positive lengths. Cylinder pressure is (p<sub>atm</sub> − ρg h<sub>s</sub>) during suction and (p<sub>atm</sub> + ρg h<sub>d</sub>) during delivery, so the pressure difference across the stroke is ρg(h<sub>d</sub> + h<sub>s</sub>). If elevations are instead taken as signed heights from the pump axis, with the suction level negative, the same bracket reads (h<sub>d</sub> − h<sub>s</sub>); say which convention you use.

blocks.text: In a real pump the suction line sags below its ideal level at the start of the stroke, because the water column must be accelerated and suction-pipe friction must be beaten; the delivery line rises above its ideal for the same reason. Both lines are wavy. The suction line dips lowest and the delivery line peaks highest near the start of each stroke, where the water column's acceleration is greatest; at mid-stroke the acceleration is zero, so the lines come back closest to the ideal levels, held apart only by friction. Valve seating takes time, so the corners are rounded. If suction-side pressure falls to the vapour pressure of water, the column separates from the piston: separation, the reciprocating pump's cavitation (see 7.5), which gives a knock and a shock when the column rejoins.

figure.caption: One crank revolution gives one suction and one delivery stroke. Geometry promises 7.634 L/s, the meter reads 6.5 L/s, and the 1.134 L/s difference is positive slip.

spec.aria: Crank and piston motion creates suction and delivery strokes; theoretical flow comes from geometry, actual flow is measured, and slip is their difference.

examples.question: A single-acting reciprocating pump has a cylinder bore of 180 mm, a stroke of 300 mm and runs at 60 rpm. Its measured discharge is 6.5 L/s. Find the theoretical discharge, the coefficient of discharge and the percentage slip.
steps: Convert to SI: D = 180 mm = 0.180 m, L = 300 mm = 0.300 m, N = 60 rpm, Q<sub>act</sub> = 6.5 L/s = 0.0065 m³/s.
Piston area A = πD²/4 = π(0.180)²/4 = 0.025447 m².
Volume swept per stroke = A L = 0.025447 × 0.300 = 7.6341 × 10⁻³ m³.
Theoretical discharge Q<sub>th</sub> = A L N/60 = 7.6341 × 10⁻³ × 60/60 = 7.634 × 10⁻³ m³/s = 7.634 L/s.
Percentage slip = 1.134 / 7.634 × 100 = 14.86 %. The slip is positive, so the pump delivers less than its geometry promises.
examples.answer: Q<sub>th</sub> = 7.634 L/s, C<sub>d</sub> = 0.851 and slip = 1.134 L/s, that is 14.86 % of the theoretical discharge.
examples.check:
import math
D = 0.180
L = 0.300
N = 60.0
Qact = 6.5e-3
A = math.pi/4*D**2
Qth = A*L*N/60
Cd = Qact/Qth
slip = Qth - Qact
print(round(A, 6))
print(round(Qth*1000, 3))
print(round(Cd, 4))
print(round(slip*1000, 3))
print(round(slip/Qth*100, 2))

traps: Using N in rpm without dividing by 60 makes Q<sub>th</sub> sixty times too large; the 60 is part of the formula.
Slip is theoretical minus actual. Positive slip means the actual discharge is smaller, so do not flip the order.
A double-acting pump uses (2A − a<sub>r</sub>), not 2A: the rod area is subtracted once, on the rod side only.
Stroke L is twice the crank radius, and both D and L must be in metres before squaring or multiplying.
C<sub>d</sub> and slip fraction add to one, so a C<sub>d</sub> of 0.92 and 8 % slip are the same statement (and a C<sub>d</sub> of 0.88 is 12 % slip).

quiz.q: State the function of the suction and delivery valves in a reciprocating pump.
quiz.a: They are one-way valves worked by pressure difference: the suction valve admits water on the outward stroke, the delivery valve passes it out on the inward stroke.

quiz.q: Why is slip normally positive in a reciprocating pump?
quiz.a: Some water leaks past valves and rings, valves take time to seat, dissolved air cushions the stroke, and at high speed the cylinder does not fill fully. Actual discharge then falls below the geometric value.

quiz.q: How can a reciprocating pump show negative slip?
quiz.a: With a long suction pipe at low speed, the water column's inertia keeps it entering after the piston has started forward, so extra water spills through the delivery valve and Q<sub>act</sub> exceeds Q<sub>th</sub>.

quiz.q: A double-acting pump has bore 250 mm, piston rod diameter 40 mm, stroke 400 mm and runs at 50 rpm. Find the theoretical discharge.
A pump has Q<sub>th</sub> = 12 L/s and C<sub>d</sub> = 0.92. Find the actual discharge and the slip.
Why does a large suction lift combined with high speed cause separation in a reciprocating pump?
quiz.a: Acceleration head grows with speed and suction pipe length, so cylinder pressure falls sharply at the start of the suction stroke. If it reaches the vapour pressure of water the column breaks away from the piston, giving a knock as it rejoins. Limit the lift and speed, or fit an air vessel.

quiz.q: The actual indicator diagram encloses more area than the ideal rectangle. What does that mean for the driving motor?
quiz.a: The extra area is net work lost to friction in the pipes, valves and piston; acceleration changes the shape of the lines but its work cancels out over a stroke. So the motor must supply more power than ρ g Q<sub>th</sub> (h<sub>d</sub> + h<sub>s</sub>). The ratio of ideal area to actual indicator-diagram area measures only what is lost inside the cylinder; the pump's overall efficiency is the water power delivered (ρ g Q<sub>act</sub> × total head) divided by the shaft power input, which is smaller still.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plunger versions of this machine push water at hundreds of bar in descaling, water jetting and reverse-osmosis desalination, where a centrifugal pump cannot reach. Dosing and metering pumps on chemical skids are reciprocating pumps with adjustable stroke length. Search 'API 674 reciprocating pumps', 'volumetric efficiency of reciprocating pump' and 'indicator diagram pump slip' to go further.
